To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) we propose a file-agnostic approach for malware family classification based on visualization of malware samples as images; and 2) we evaluate our method on two benchmark datasets and compare its results to those of state-of-the-art approaches.

(1) the use of convolutional neural networks to classify malware as images outperforms state-of-the-art malware classification approaches; (2) the use of a file agnostic approach to visualize malware as images is more efficient and effective than using a file agnostic image generation approach; (3) the use of gray scale images instead of RGB color images improves classification results.

(1) we use a deep learning approach to detect and classify malware families, (2) we use a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture to extract features from the image representations of malicious files, (3) we achieve state-of-the-art performance, and (4) we show that our approach is able to detect malware variants that are not detected by state-of-the-art approaches
